options.a: The central claim the author develops
options.b: The topic the passage mentions most often
options.c: The first sentence of the opening paragraph
options.d: The most memorable example the author gives

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses topic with main idea; the topic is the subject, while the main idea is the claim the author makes about it.
distractorExplanations.c: The main idea is not always stated first; it may be implied or appear later, so position alone does not define it.
distractorExplanations.d: Examples are supporting details; choosing a vivid example over the overarching claim is a classic main-idea trap.

options.a: State the author's central claim
options.b: Explain or prove the main idea
options.c: Introduce a new topic for the next paragraph
options.d: Present the opposing view

distractorExplanations.a: That is the job of the thesis or main idea itself; supporting details back up that claim rather than state it.
distractorExplanations.c: Introducing the next topic is a transition's role; a supporting detail develops the current main idea with evidence.
distractorExplanations.d: That is a counterargument; supporting details advance the author's own main idea rather than the opposing view.

options.a: A fact the author states directly in the passage
options.b: A personal opinion based on the reader's experience
options.c: A conclusion backed by the text but not stated outright
options.d: A summary that restates the passage's main points

distractorExplanations.a: An explicitly stated fact requires no inference; inferring means drawing a conclusion the text supports but does not say.
distractorExplanations.b: Inferences must rest on textual evidence, not on the reader's own experience or opinions from outside the passage.
distractorExplanations.d: Summarizing restates what is explicitly said; an inference goes a step beyond the stated text using its evidence.

options.a: Objective — reviews avoid judging the work
options.b: Nostalgic — reviews dwell on the author's past works
options.c: Ambivalent — reviewers withhold any verdict
options.d: Evaluative — look at charged verbs and qualifiers

distractorExplanations.a: Critical reviews exist to judge a work; an objective tone fits reports or summaries, not evaluative reviews.
distractorExplanations.b: Nostalgia is a wistful tone about the past; a critical review's tone is evaluative, weighing strengths and flaws.
distractorExplanations.c: Ambivalence means undecided feelings; a critical review usually delivers a judgment through charged wording.

options.a: The meaning that fits this sentence
options.b: The word's most common dictionary definition
options.c: The meaning of the word's Latin root
options.d: A synonym that sounds most formal

distractorExplanations.b: The most common meaning is often the trap; vocabulary-in-context items reward the sense the sentence requires.
distractorExplanations.c: Roots can hint, but the item asks how the word is used in this sentence, which may differ from its etymology.
distractorExplanations.d: Formality is not the criterion; the correct choice is the meaning that fits the specific sentence context.

options.a: Events presented in the order they occurred
options.b: Similarities and differences between two things
options.c: A problem followed by one or more solutions
options.d: Reasons why an event happened and its results

distractorExplanations.a: That is chronological (sequence) structure; compare-contrast weighs how two things are alike and different.
distractorExplanations.c: That is problem-solution structure; compare-contrast is signaled by words like 'similarly', 'unlike', 'however'.
distractorExplanations.d: That describes cause-effect structure; compare-contrast examines similarities and differences between subjects.

options.a: How two subjects are alike and different
options.b: Steps listed in the exact order they occurred
options.c: Why something happened or what it produced
options.d: An issue and the proposed ways to fix it

distractorExplanations.a: That is compare-contrast structure; cause-effect explains reasons and results, signaled by 'because' or 'therefore'.
distractorExplanations.b: Sequence structure orders events in time; cause-effect links events by explaining why they happened or what followed.
distractorExplanations.d: That is problem-solution structure; cause-effect focuses on reasons and consequences rather than proposed fixes.

options.a: Choose the passage with stronger credentials
options.b: Assume the more recent passage is correct
options.c: Summarize each passage's topic separately
options.d: Identify the exact point of difference

distractorExplanations.a: Paired-passage items ask how the views differ, not which author is more credentialed; judge the claims in the text.
distractorExplanations.b: Publication date does not settle the question; identify precisely where and why the two authors disagree.
distractorExplanations.c: Separate summaries miss the relationship; the task is to pinpoint the specific claim on which the passages differ.

options.a: From the time, by a participant or witness
options.b: A later historian's analysis of the period
options.c: A modern textbook that quotes eyewitnesses
options.d: A documentary film made about the era

distractorExplanations.b: A historian writing afterward produces a secondary source; primary sources come from participants at the time.
distractorExplanations.c: Quoting eyewitnesses does not make a textbook primary; it remains a secondary source that interprets the past.
distractorExplanations.d: A later documentary interprets events from outside the period, which makes it a secondary source, not a primary one.

options.a: A statistic drawn from a large random sample
options.b: An anecdote treated as proof of a general rule
options.c: A quotation from a recognized expert in the field
options.d: Results replicated across several controlled studies

distractorExplanations.a: A large random-sample statistic is strong evidence; the weakness is generalizing from a single anecdote.
distractorExplanations.c: Relevant expert testimony generally strengthens an argument; an isolated anecdote is the weakest support.
distractorExplanations.d: Replicated controlled studies are among the strongest evidence, the opposite of a lone anecdote generalized.

options.a: State the thesis in a shortened form
options.b: Summarize the main idea of the section
options.c: Credit a source or add a narrow aside
options.d: Define every key term for the reader

distractorExplanations.a: The thesis belongs in the body text; a footnote cites a source or adds a minor side comment.
distractorExplanations.b: Summaries belong in the text or headings; footnotes handle source credit or narrow asides outside the main flow.
distractorExplanations.d: Key definitions usually appear in the text or a glossary; footnotes are for citations and narrow side notes.

options.a: Replace close reading for detail questions
options.b: Read all the answer choices before the passage itself
options.c: Memorize names and dates before the questions
options.d: Map structure before close reading the item's lines

distractorExplanations.a: Skimming cannot answer detail items by itself; it builds a structural map so you know where to read closely.
distractorExplanations.b: Previewing choices is a different tactic; skimming means quickly surveying the passage to map its structure.
distractorExplanations.c: Memorizing details wastes time; skimming targets the passage's structure so details can be located later.

options.a: Evidence you must read as carefully as prose
options.b: Background you can skip unless numbers appear
options.c: A restatement of the passage you can ignore
options.d: Evidence that overrides the passage's claims

distractorExplanations.b: Graphs in Core sets carry testable evidence; skipping them loses information that questions directly ask about.
distractorExplanations.c: Graphs often add data the text lacks; treating them as redundant misses questions that integrate both sources.
distractorExplanations.d: A graph is one source among others; read it alongside the text rather than letting it override the prose.

options.a: It is right if it is widely known
options.b: It is wrong for this test
options.c: It is right if the topic matches
options.d: It earns partial credit on the test

distractorExplanations.a: Outside knowledge does not count; answers must be supported by the passage even when they are true in the world.
distractorExplanations.c: Matching the topic is not enough; the choice must be supported by what this particular passage actually says.
distractorExplanations.d: Praxis Core multiple-choice items give no partial credit; a choice the passage does not support is simply wrong.

options.a: The official ETS Praxis Core practice form
options.b: Practice for Praxis Elementary Education (5001)
options.c: Independent academic-skills practice
options.d: A teaching-methods and pedagogy review

distractorExplanations.a: This is an independent UniPrep diagnostic, not an official ETS form; official practice tests come from ETS.
distractorExplanations.b: Praxis Elementary Education covers K-6 content and pedagogy; Core tests reading, writing, and math skills.
distractorExplanations.d: Pedagogy is tested by PLT and content tests, not Core; Core measures academic reading, writing, and math.

options.a: A broad statement of the topic
options.b: A widely accepted fact
options.c: A question for the reader
options.d: A debatable, specific claim

distractorExplanations.a: A topic announcement takes no position; a thesis must make a specific claim that a reader could dispute.
distractorExplanations.b: Facts no one disputes cannot be argued; a thesis must be debatable so the essay has something to prove.
distractorExplanations.c: A question raises an issue without taking a stand; a thesis answers it with a specific, arguable claim.

options.a: 'The list of items are'
options.b: 'The list of items is'
options.c: 'Each of the students has'
options.d: 'Neither the coach nor the players are'

distractorExplanations.b: This sentence is correct: the subject is 'list' (singular), so 'is' agrees; 'of items' is only a prepositional phrase.
distractorExplanations.c: 'Each' is singular, so 'has' agrees correctly; the plural 'students' in the phrase is a common trap for the ear.
distractorExplanations.d: With neither/nor, the verb agrees with the nearer subject, 'players', so 'are' is correct in this sentence.

options.a: A dependent clause set off by a comma
options.b: Two independents joined by only a comma
options.c: Two independents joined by a semicolon
options.d: Two independents joined with no punctuation

distractorExplanations.a: An introductory dependent clause followed by a comma is correct; a splice joins two independent clauses with a comma.
distractorExplanations.c: A semicolon correctly joins two independent clauses; the comma splice error is joining them with a comma alone.
distractorExplanations.d: Two independent clauses with no punctuation at all form a fused (run-on) sentence, not a comma splice.

options.a: It is an adverb placed next to its verb
options.b: It appears at the start of the sentence
options.c: It is separated from the verb by a comma
options.d: It sits next to the wrong noun

distractorExplanations.a: An adverb next to the verb it modifies is correctly placed; misplacement means the modifier attaches to the wrong word.
distractorExplanations.b: Opening modifiers are fine when the noun right after them is what they describe; position alone is not the error.
distractorExplanations.c: Commas around modifiers are often required; the problem is a modifier sitting beside the wrong noun.

options.a: The same grammatical shape in a list
options.b: List items ordered by length
options.c: A mix of forms to add variety to the list
options.d: A comma before the last item of a list

distractorExplanations.b: Ordering by length is a style choice; parallelism requires each list item to share the same grammatical form.
distractorExplanations.c: Mixing a gerund, an infinitive, and a clause in one list is exactly the faulty parallelism the rule forbids.
distractorExplanations.d: That is the serial (Oxford) comma, a punctuation choice; parallelism is about matching grammatical structure.

options.a: Its = it is; it's = possession
options.b: It's = it is; its = possession
options.c: It's = possession; its' = plural
options.d: Both forms show possession

distractorExplanations.a: Reverses the pair: the apostrophe in it's marks the contraction of 'it is', while possessive its has none.
distractorExplanations.c: Its' is not a word, and it's is not possessive; it's means 'it is' (or 'it has') and its shows possession.
distractorExplanations.d: Only its is possessive; it's is the contraction of 'it is' or 'it has', so the two forms are not interchangeable.

options.a: Closes the paragraph by summarizing the essay
options.b: Presents a quotation that supports the thesis
options.c: Opens the paragraph with the paragraph's point
options.d: Restates the thesis word for word in each paragraph

distractorExplanations.a: That describes a concluding sentence; a topic sentence usually opens the paragraph by stating its point.
distractorExplanations.b: Quotations are supporting evidence within the paragraph; the topic sentence states the paragraph's main point.
distractorExplanations.d: Topic sentences connect to the thesis but state each paragraph's own point; repeating the thesis verbatim is weak.

options.a: Transitions that link the ideas
options.b: Specific examples that support claims
options.c: Technical terms the audience needs
options.d: Empty intensifiers and doubled words

distractorExplanations.a: Transitions aid coherence and should stay; concision cuts empty words like 'very' and redundant pairs.
distractorExplanations.b: Examples are substantive support; concision removes filler and redundancy, not evidence that develops the argument.
distractorExplanations.c: Necessary terminology carries meaning; concision targets empty intensifiers and doubled phrasing like 'each and every'.

options.a: You use someone else's words or distinctive facts
options.b: You state widely known common knowledge
options.c: You present your own original argument
options.d: You give your own definition of a common term

distractorExplanations.b: Common knowledge, such as well-known dates, does not need a citation; borrowed words and distinctive facts do.
distractorExplanations.c: Your own analysis and claims need no citation; credit is required for borrowed words, ideas, or facts.
distractorExplanations.d: Defining a common term in your own words is your work; citations are owed for others' words or distinctive facts.

options.a: It is used in a lab report's methods section
options.b: It hides the actor you should name
options.c: The receiver of the action is the focus
options.d: The actor is unknown or unimportant

distractorExplanations.a: Passive voice is conventional in scientific methods sections where the actor is unimportant; that use is acceptable.
distractorExplanations.c: Passive is appropriate when the receiver is the focus; the problem is using it to obscure a responsible actor.
distractorExplanations.d: When the actor is unknown or irrelevant, passive voice is acceptable; it is a problem when it hides a needed actor.

options.a: A full independent clause ending in a period
options.b: Two sentences joined with only a comma
options.c: A dependent piece punctuated as a sentence
options.d: A sentence with a misplaced modifier

distractorExplanations.a: A complete independent clause is a sentence; a fragment lacks a subject, a verb, or a complete thought.
distractorExplanations.b: That is a comma splice; a fragment is an incomplete piece punctuated as though it were a full sentence.
distractorExplanations.d: A misplaced modifier is a placement error inside a complete sentence; a fragment is not a complete sentence.

options.a: Claim, reasons, evidence, and a response to a counterpoint
options.b: A personal narrative that builds to a lesson
options.c: A neutral summary of both sides with no verdict
options.d: A list of facts about the topic followed by a concluding quote

distractorExplanations.b: Narratives suit personal essays; an argumentative essay needs a claim supported by reasons, evidence, and rebuttal.
distractorExplanations.c: Presenting both sides without a position makes an informative piece; an argument must take and defend a claim.
distractorExplanations.d: Facts without a claim and reasons do not argue; the essay must tie evidence to a position and answer counterpoints.

options.a: Effect is the verb; affect is the noun
options.b: Affect is the verb; effect is the noun
options.c: Both are verbs with interchangeable meanings
options.d: Affect is the adjective; effect is the adverb

distractorExplanations.a: Reverses the usual pair: affect is normally the verb ('to influence') and effect the noun ('a result').
distractorExplanations.c: In usual use they are not interchangeable; affect is the verb and effect the noun, apart from rare special senses.
distractorExplanations.d: Neither is normally an adjective or adverb (those are 'affective' and 'effectively'); affect is the verb, effect the noun.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats 3:4 as the fraction 3/4 of the whole; the parts are 3/7 and 4/7 because the ratio has 3 + 4 = 7 parts.
distractorExplanations.b: Mixes two methods: 12 is right, but the second part must be 4/7 of 28 = 16 so that the parts sum to 28.
distractorExplanations.d: Multiplies the whole by each ratio term instead of splitting it; the parts of 28 must themselves add up to 28.

options.a: Halves distance
options.b: Squares distance
options.c: Doubles distance
options.d: Leaves distance

distractorExplanations.a: “Halves distance” does not answer “A proportional word problem that doubles time at the same rate:”. The matching answer is: Doubles distance.
distractorExplanations.b: “Squares distance” does not answer “A proportional word problem that doubles time at the same rate:”. The matching answer is: Doubles distance.
distractorExplanations.d: “Leaves distance” does not answer “A proportional word problem that doubles time at the same rate:”. The matching answer is: Doubles distance.

options.a: 3.33 approximately (10/3)
options.b: 5 exactly (20/4)
options.c: 6 exactly (the median value)
options.d: 6.67 approximately (20/3)

distractorExplanations.a: Uses a sum of 10, dropping one value; the full sum is 4 + 6 + 10 = 20, so the mean is 20/3, about 6.67.
distractorExplanations.b: Divides the sum by 4 instead of by the count of values, 3; the mean of 4, 6, 10 is 20/3, about 6.67.
distractorExplanations.c: 6 is the median, the middle value; the mean is the sum divided by the count, 20/3, about 6.67.

distractorExplanations.a: “13” does not answer “Area of a rectangle 5 by 8 is:”. The matching answer is: 40.
distractorExplanations.b: “26” does not answer “Area of a rectangle 5 by 8 is:”. The matching answer is: 40.
distractorExplanations.d: “80” does not answer “Area of a rectangle 5 by 8 is:”. The matching answer is: 40.

distractorExplanations.a: 3/4 is the chance of not drawing red (the complement); the red chance is 1 favorable out of 4 total marbles.
distractorExplanations.b: 1/3 comes from the odds of 1 red to 3 non-red; probability divides by the total of 4, giving 1/4.
distractorExplanations.c: Uses 5 as the total by counting the red marble again; the 4 marbles already include it, so the chance is 1/4.

distractorExplanations.b: 320 is 3.2 × 10^2; multiplying by 10^3 moves the decimal three places to the right, giving 3200.
distractorExplanations.c: 3.2 ignores the power of ten; 10^3 means multiplying by 1,000, so 3.2 × 10^3 equals 3200.
distractorExplanations.d: 0.0032 is 3.2 × 10^-3; a positive exponent moves the decimal to the right, not the left, giving 3200.

options.a: Divide by −2, keeping x > −4
options.b: Divide by −2, so x < −4
options.c: Divide by 2, giving −x < 4
options.d: Add 2x, so 0 < 8 + 2x

distractorExplanations.a: Dividing both sides by a negative number reverses the inequality; keeping '>' gives the wrong solution set.
distractorExplanations.c: Dividing by positive 2 does not flip the sign; it gives −x > 4, and the flip happens when dividing by −2.
distractorExplanations.d: Adding the same term to both sides keeps the direction (0 > 8 + 2x); only multiplying or dividing by a negative flips it.

distractorExplanations.a: 60 is the number of minutes in one hour; 2 hours is 2 × 60 = 120 minutes.
distractorExplanations.b: Treats an hour as 100 minutes (decimal thinking); an hour has 60 minutes, so 2 hours is 120 minutes.
distractorExplanations.d: 7,200 is the number of seconds in 2 hours (2 × 3,600), not minutes; in minutes it is 2 × 60 = 120.

distractorExplanations.a: 12 is the area of one 3 × 4 face; volume multiplies all three dimensions, so 2 × 3 × 4 = 24.
distractorExplanations.b: Adds the face products 2 × 3 and 2 × 4 instead of multiplying all three dimensions; volume is 2 × 3 × 4 = 24.
distractorExplanations.c: Adds the face areas 2 × 3 and 3 × 4 rather than multiplying length × width × height, which gives 24.

options.a: A positive association
options.b: A negative association
options.c: No association between the variables
options.d: Proof that one variable causes the other

distractorExplanations.b: A negative association falls to the right; points rising from left to right show a positive association.
distractorExplanations.c: No association would show a shapeless cloud; a rising pattern indicates the variables increase together.
distractorExplanations.d: A scatterplot shows correlation; a rising trend alone cannot establish that one variable causes the other.

options.a: Work every item strictly in the order presented
options.b: Answer easy items first and mark hard ones to return
options.c: Leave hard items blank since wrong answers cost points
options.d: Give each item the same time before moving on

distractorExplanations.a: Rigid order lets one hard item drain time from easier points; flag hard items and come back to them later.
distractorExplanations.c: Praxis Core has no guessing penalty; blank answers earn nothing, so answer every item before time ends.
distractorExplanations.d: Fixed equal timing wastes minutes on hard items; answering easy ones first banks points and leaves time to return.

options.a: Checking which answer choice looks closest
options.b: Finding the relationship the problem describes
options.c: Arithmetic you already set up
options.d: Estimating answers you cannot set up

distractorExplanations.a: Punching answer choices into the calculator without a setup is guessing; it computes arithmetic you planned.
distractorExplanations.b: The calculator cannot identify the relationship; you set up the equation first, then use it to compute.
distractorExplanations.d: If you cannot set up the problem, a calculator will not rescue it; it is a tool for computing an existing setup.

options.a: The test deducts points for wrong answers
options.b: The correct answer is usually the longest choice
options.c: You can then skip reading the passage
options.d: You raise the odds on the remaining pair

distractorExplanations.a: Praxis Core has no wrong-answer penalty; elimination helps because a guess between two choices is a 50% chance.
distractorExplanations.b: Length is not a reliable signal on Praxis; elimination works because removing wrong choices improves the odds.
distractorExplanations.c: Elimination still relies on the passage; you cut choices the text contradicts, then compare the last two against it.

options.a: Apply a named rule (agreement, comma, parallel)
options.b: Choose the one that sounds more formal
options.c: Pick the shorter one because concision wins
options.d: Read both aloud and trust your ear

distractorExplanations.b: Formality is not correctness; pick the option that satisfies a specific rule such as agreement or parallelism.
distractorExplanations.c: Concision matters after correctness; a shorter option can still break agreement or punctuation rules.
distractorExplanations.d: The ear misleads when both options sound natural; the tie-breaker is checking each against a named grammar rule.

options.a: Trust the picture's lengths and angles
options.b: Do not measure with your pencil — use the given numbers
options.c: Assume right angles wherever corners look square on the page
options.d: The given numbers may also be inaccurate

distractorExplanations.a: Not drawn to scale means the picture's proportions are unreliable; rely on the stated measurements instead.
distractorExplanations.c: Angles that look like 90 degrees may not be; assume a right angle only when it is marked or stated.
distractorExplanations.d: The numbers and labels are reliable; it is the drawing's proportions that are not, so compute from the given values.

options.a: Starting to write right away to save time
options.b: Restating the prompt as the opening paragraph
options.c: A 1-minute outline of claim + two reasons
options.d: Memorizing a full essay to adapt on test day

distractorExplanations.a: Skipping planning leads to a disorganized essay; a quick outline of claim and reasons saves time overall.
distractorExplanations.b: Copying the prompt adds no argument; a brief outline of a claim and two reasons gives the essay its structure.
distractorExplanations.d: Pre-written essays rarely fit the actual prompt; a fresh 1-minute outline addresses the question actually asked.

options.a: Using the original value as the base for the change
options.b: Dividing the change by the original value, not the new one
options.c: Converting the percent to a decimal before multiplying
options.d: Adding the percent to 100 incorrectly or using the wrong base

distractorExplanations.a: Using the original value as the base is the correct method for percent increase, so it is not the trap.
distractorExplanations.b: Change divided by original is exactly the right percent-increase formula; the trap is using the new value instead.
distractorExplanations.c: Converting the percent to a decimal is a correct step; the trap is a wrong base or mishandling the 100% total.

options.a: Solved in one step from the last sentence
options.b: Skipped because it takes too much time
options.c: Rewritten as small equations
options.d: Answered by estimating from the figure

distractorExplanations.a: Multi-step items hide intermediate quantities; jumping to the last sentence skips the steps that produce the answer.
distractorExplanations.b: Multi-step items count the same as others and are often solvable; break them into steps rather than skipping.
distractorExplanations.d: Estimating from a figure is unreliable, especially one not drawn to scale; write out each step as an equation.

options.a: Misread a word in the passage
options.b: Choose an answer the passage doesn't support
options.c: Solve for the wrong variable in an equation
options.d: Copy the wrong bubble — check the number

distractorExplanations.a: Misreading is a comprehension error; a transfer error happens when a correct answer is marked in the wrong spot.
distractorExplanations.b: That is a reasoning error; transfer errors are clerical, marking an answer next to the wrong question number.
distractorExplanations.c: Solving for the wrong quantity is a setup error; a transfer error is recording a right answer in the wrong place.

options.a: Short items and graphs first, then leftover long prose
options.b: Start the longest remaining passage from the very top
options.c: Reread your earlier answers to double-check them
options.d: Leave the remaining items blank to avoid errors

distractorExplanations.b: A long passage eats the remaining minutes for few points; triage short items and graphs first instead.
distractorExplanations.c: Rechecking can wait; with time nearly gone, answer unattempted quick items first so no points are left blank.
distractorExplanations.d: Praxis Core has no guessing penalty, so blanks earn nothing; answer every remaining item, quick ones first.

options.a: Your scratch work from the first attempt at the problem
options.b: What the question asked (solve vs evaluate vs simplify)
options.c: The answer choices to see which one looks closest
options.d: The units used in the answer choices

distractorExplanations.a: Scratch work can repeat the same mistake; first confirm what the question asked, since that sets the target.
distractorExplanations.c: Starting with the choices invites guessing; re-read the stem to confirm whether to solve, evaluate, or simplify.
distractorExplanations.d: Units matter, but the first check is what the question asked; solving for x when it asked for 2x is the common miss.

options.a: The option most true in the real world
options.b: The option that repeats the passage's wording
options.c: The most complete, passage-faithful option
options.d: The option with the most specific detail

distractorExplanations.a: Real-world truth is not the standard; the best answer is the one the passage most fully supports.
distractorExplanations.b: Copied wording is a frequent trap; the best answer captures the passage's meaning, often in different words.
distractorExplanations.d: A narrow detail can be true but incomplete; the best answer covers what the question asks most fully.

options.a: A test of reading comprehension skills
options.b: A test of grammar and essay writing
options.c: A test of algebra, geometry, and data skills
options.d: A test of classroom management or lesson plans

distractorExplanations.a: Reading is one of the three Core subtests, so it is part of Praxis Core rather than something Core excludes.
distractorExplanations.b: Writing, including grammar items and essays, is a Core subtest; pedagogy and lesson planning are what Core excludes.
distractorExplanations.c: Mathematics (number, algebra, geometry, data) is a Core subtest; classroom management belongs to PLT and similar tests.
